ARTICLE IN PRESS The utilization level of medical resources, health capital and financial asset allocation of middle-aged and elderly households Abstract Addressing the challenges of aging and fostering a healthy China necessitates redefining the socioeconomic role of middle-aged and elderly individuals. Despite the close link between the distribution of household financial assets and financial market stability, few studies have examined S the low participation of middle-aged and elderly households inS financial markets through the lens E of medical resource utilization. This study was conductedR to analyze the influence of the utilization P level of medical resources and health capital on the financial asset allocation of these households, N I exploring the underlying mechanisms and d ifferential impacts. Utilizing the 2015 and 2018 China E L Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) datasets, this study empirically assessed C I the impacts of medical resource utilization and health capital on financial asset allocation via logit T R and Tobit models. A mAediating effect model was employed to delve into the mechanisms of action. The findings indicate that medical resource utilization and health capital positively impact the financial market participation and risky asset holdings of middle-aged and elderly households, and these findings are robust. Regarding the mechanisms of action, medical resources influence allocation via health capital. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that the effects on high-income and urban households are more obvious, whereas those on middle- and low-income and rural households are not. This study offers a foundation for policy decisions promoting the coordinated development of a healthy China and the financing of the aging population. Recommendations ARTICLE IN PRESS include expanding primary medical services, enhancing households’ health capital, advancing financial reform and innovation, optimizing the asset allocation of middle-aged and elderly households, and addressing urban‒rural income disparities to facilitate societal and economic health. JSON: Name: medical_resource_health_finance_pipeline Title: Double-hurdle, instrumental-variable, and mediation analysis of how medical resource utilization and health capital affect financial asset allocation of middle-aged and elderly households Short Hypothesis: Increased utilization of primary medical resources raises household health capital, which in turn increases (a) the probability that middle-aged and elderly households participate in risky financial assets and (b) the share of risky assets in their financial portfolios. Related Work: Existing empirical work links individual or household health shocks and health capital to reductions in risky asset participation and shifts toward liquid or low-risk holdings. Typical methods include cross-sectional and panel regressions, Tobit or two-part models for censored asset shares, and instrumental-variable approaches to address endogeneity. Prior studies often measure health via self-reports or single objective indicators and treat medical care as an expenditure shock rather than as a resource-utilization process. Limitations in prior approaches include: (1) conflating participation and intensity decisions by using single-equation Tobit or OLS, (2) incomplete treatment of endogeneity between health and asset choice, (3) limited exploration of medical resource utilization as an antecedent of health capital and a mediator for financial behavior, (4) insufficient robustness checks for zero-inflation and overdispersion in visit-count measures, and (5) sparse heterogeneity analysis across income and urban/rural registration. Abstract: This research pipeline specifies an empirical program to test whether and how the utilization level of medical resources affects financial asset allocation among middle-aged and elderly households through health capital. Using household-level survey data, we operationalize utilization with visit counts and hospital-tier indicators and health capital with both subjective health and an objective health-quality index. The core empirical strategy models a two-stage decision process (participation and conditional share) via a double-hurdle estimator, implements instrumental-variable estimation for health endogeneity using community-average health, and quantifies mediation through causal mediation/structural equation techniques. We will run robustness checks including winsorization, alternative health measures (mental health/depression scale), and exclusion of loans from the risky-asset definition. Primary outputs are marginal effects on participation, changes in risky-asset share, mediation proportions attributable to health capital, and heterogeneity by income and hukou. Expected outcomes include quantifying the mediated effect of medical-resource utilization on risky investment behavior and identifying population subgroups for targeted policy design. Experiments: Datasets: CHARLS waves 2015 and 2018; sample restricted to household heads aged 45–80; final pooled cross-section n≈1,888 after cleaning. Dependent variables: (1) participation indicator = 1 if household holds any risky financial asset (stocks, funds, loans) ; (2) risky_share = risky financial assets / total financial assets. Core exposures: monthly_outpatient_visits (count), annual_hospitalizations (count), primary_care_visits (count), large_hospital_visits (count). Mediator: health_capital measured as (A) self_reported_health binary and (B) health_quality_index (Kaplan–Anderson method). Control covariates: age, education, hukou, family size, log annual income, log annual expenditure, food expenditure, medical insurance, year fixed effects, community fixed effects. Primary models: (a) double-hurdle (Cragg) with first-stage probit/logit for participation and truncated-normal for positive risky_share; (b) Tobit and two-part model for comparison; (c) IV-double-hurdle: first-stage OLS regressions of health_capital on instrument community_avg_health to obtain fitted mediator; second-stage double-hurdle with fitted health; (d) causal mediation analysis / structural equation model to estimate mediation proportion and direct/indirect effects. Baselines: naive OLS/Tobit without mediation; logit for participation only; double-hurdle without IV. Instrumental variable: community-average health (mean self_reported_health and mean health_quality within community). Robustness and ablations: (1) winsorize top/bottom 5% of continuous variables; (2) replace health_capital with CES-D depression score; (3) log-transform counts and alternate models using negative-binomial for counts; (4) redefine risky assets excluding loans and re-estimate all models; (5) compare double-hurdle vs Tobit vs two-part via AIC/BIC and out-of-sample predictive checks. Heterogeneity: stratified analyses by income (below/above median) and hukou (rural/urban). Evaluation metrics and diagnostics: coefficient estimates and clustered robust SEs (cluster = community), marginal effects, average treatment effects (ATE) for utilization changes, mediation proportion and confidence intervals (bootstrap 1,000 draws), first-stage F-statistic (>10 threshold), overidentification/Hansen tests if multiple instruments available, pseudo-R2, AIC/BIC, model log-likelihood, and calibration plots for participation predictions. Reporting: effect sizes with 95% CIs, p-values, and sensitivity analysis to alternative instrument definitions. Risk Factors and Limitations: Data limitations: CHARLS provides repeated cross-sections but not continuous panel for all households; latest post-2018 shocks (e.g., COVID-19) are not captured. Measurement error: utilization counts and self-reported health are subject to recall bias; the constructed health_quality_index uses weights from prior work that may not fit current population. Endogeneity and instrument validity: community-average health may violate exclusion if community health correlates with unobserved local economic factors that also affect asset choices. Statistical power: low prevalence of risky-asset holders (≈6%) reduces power for subgroup analyses and increases standard errors. Model specification risks: double-hurdle distributional assumptions (truncated-normal) may be misspecified; count overdispersion may bias estimates if not modeled properly. Generalizability: findings may not transfer to other countries or younger cohorts due to institutional differences in medical and financial systems. Operational constraints: clustering at community level reduces effective sample size for inference; winsorization and exclusion rules can affect effect magnitudes. Computational: bootstrap mediation inference with IV and double-hurdle is computationally intensive and may require substantial compute resources.
